brief.head: Bills as big data
brief.text: Offered a hero who steals his neighbours’ bills, Ajay Shah saw only one earthly reason to do it: “to create a data set about electricity consumption.” {079-J01}

brief.head: Dear sister-in-law
brief.text: Bota Singh’s taunting verse letter to Zakaria Khan addressed the governor as “my sister-in-law”. Amit Varma admitted he did not quite understand why that was an insult. {079-J12}

brief.head: A governor with no OTT
brief.text: Why would a governor used to fifty thousand horses ride out against two men? No wars, said Amit Varma, and “no OTTs to watch. So Zakaria Khan is bored.” {079-J11}

brief.head: No more Indians
brief.text: As Amit Varma remembers it, after RB Ramesh and then Abhijit Kunte won the British Chess Championship, the organisers barred Indians. Today, he said, the top ten would be Indian. {079-J17}

brief.head: I am the parcel
brief.text: A friend of Amit Varma’s in Bangalore, unable to get an Uber, booked a Dunzo parcel delivery and told the rider: “I am the parcel.” {079-J19}

thought.who: Ajay Shah, setting up his true story of children sent through the post

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah pitch four more films
lead.head: Bills, a bridge, a board and a boy
body: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah have pitched stories that should be films in several episodes. None of them has been made into a film yet. So Varma opened this one with an offer: “If you, gentle reader, are interested in producing a film like that, get in touch with us, we’ll get the job done.” {079-R08}
This time there were four pitches: a man who steals his neighbours’ electricity bills, two young Sikhs who seize a bridge, two chess players across a board, and a child sent through the post.
Three were Varma’s, built from the inside out: backstory, motive, glances and props. The fourth was Shah’s, whose idea of a film, he said, is “exactly opposite”.
## A thief with a heart
The first began with a dream. The show’s cinematographer, Vaishnav Vyas, dreamt that Shah was stealing everyone’s paperwork. Varma kept the premise and built a quiet love story on it.

His hero is a geeky bachelor in his early fifties who looks like Shah. He picks up his neighbours’ bills from their doorsteps. A friend in the electricity department cuts off those who forget to pay, and “Ajay Bhai” gets the power back for the bill amount, a late fee and a bribe.
Then a woman moves in, too ill to leave her bed, and the grifter softens. “He is human,” Varma said. “He is touched by this.” {079-S01}
Shah suggested grounding the hero in the Marxist idea of alienation. Varma preferred to let the why show through in how the characters live.
## A toll of their own

The second pitch was history, from Sarbpreet Singh’s *Cauldron, Sword and Victory*. In 1739, with the Sikhs in hiding from Zakaria Khan, the Mughal governor of Punjab, two young Sikhs, Bota Singh and Garja Singh, took an empty bridge on the road from Delhi to Lahore.
They taxed every traveller, taunted the governor into riding out, and died fighting, with one working leg between them.

Varma kept the events and invented only the inner lives: a black sheep, a rejected suitor, two young men who did not know what they wanted. He turned their deaths into a question for everyone: what futile battles are we fighting? {079-S02}
The third pitch put the real Sultan Khan, an Indian who won the British Chess Championship in 1928, across the board from Mr B, the prisoner in Stefan Zweig’s novella *The Royal Game*.
In Varma’s ending, Khan becomes world champion, then lets Mr B win, seeing that the game he had played all his life was never the one on the board. {079-S03}
## Return to sender

Shah’s story was true. In 19th-century America, he said, the post office would carry a parcel anywhere in the country at modest prices, and one day someone asked to post a child. The clerks weighed the child, charged the parcel rate and pasted the address on the child’s shirt. {079-S05}
Posting children soon became normal. For Shah, it showed how far parents, postal workers and children trusted strangers. “It speaks very well for the trust capital of that country,” he said.
Varma, asked to bring the premise to life, supplied a drunk father, a storm and a lonely old man in a sorting office.
That, Shah said, is how they divide the work: he sets up “the rules of a situation”, and it takes “a genius like you” to animate it.

second.label: Bragging rights
second.head: Beat a grandmaster, once
second.deck: Amit Varma’s favourite boast, and the fine print he usually leaves out
body: Amit Varma often boasts that he has beaten a grandmaster. It is, he admitted, “a very dishonest boast”: he was 17, and the boy across the board was 14 and not yet a grandmaster. {#kunte}

The boy was Abhijit Kunte, at a chess club in Pune. He went on to become a grandmaster, Indian champion and British champion. Varma beat him in one blitz game with a queen sacrifice, and Kunte said: “My God, I didn’t know you could play like this.” {#queensac}
They must have played dozens of blitz games, Varma said, and he surely lost all the rest. “It is sweet joy to win even once.” {079-S04}

quote.text: I will often boast that I have beaten one grandmaster in my life.

second.caption: his one blitz win over Abhijit Kunte

third.head: Lions, at any price
body: A thread ran through Amit Varma’s pitches: people who fight, sometimes to the death, to prove something to others and to themselves.
Bota Singh and Garja Singh seized a bridge, and died on it, because a farmer had called them jackals rather than lions. A real lion, the farmer said, would never run away or hide.
Varma’s Sultan Khan has to win every game, almost on demand, because everywhere respect is at stake: “His respect, his father’s respect, his family’s respect, his nation’s respect.” {#respect}

“So many lives are lost because you’re anxious to prove things to others, because you’re anxious to prove things to yourself,” Varma said. {079-C06} Then he went further: “Is everything is everything a futile battle?”
third.caption: battles fought for respect

p2.title: The director’s cut
p2.deck: Craft, rent, respect and trust: what the four pitches argue, chapter by chapter

sections.label: First reel
sections.head: Show, don’t spell it out
sections.caption: showing, not telling
body: Amit Varma set up his first film with props, not speeches. The hero’s life is set out in a glance: wires and electronics everywhere, storage boxes full of paper, one toaster, half a packet of bread and piles and piles of Maggi packets. {#maggi}
“I’m doing a show don’t tell kind of thing here,” Varma said. Even the hero’s tea is dip-dip tea.

When the hero promises his ailing neighbour dal chawal, he remembers that he cannot cook, botches it and gets some from elsewhere. She realises as she eats that he cannot have made it. {#dalrealise} They look at each other and smile. Nothing is spelt out.
## Where the why goes
Ajay Shah wanted the hero’s motive grounded in the Marxist idea of alienation. Varma disagreed: the why should come through in how characters live and act, not be stated outright. {079-C02}

Her neatness, shown in her painstaking cooking, pays off in his bathroom, where she cannot leave a cupboard half-open. It “springs back out like an adamant economist,” Varma said, and then further, “like a recalcitrant communist”. {079-J03}

~ The hero’s hoarding, the film reveals, began as a compulsion: he sees paper on a doorstep and can’t help himself. Then, as Varma put it, “somebody’s electricity is cut and he offers to help and out of this emerges the business model.”

quote.text: I think a mistake that mainstream films often make is they try to locate the why.

sections.label: Second reel
sections.head: Hafta on the high road
sections.caption: rent-seeking on the bridge
body: Amit Varma’s first two pitches are both small studies of rent-seeking. His bill collector creates a problem and then charges to solve it. “The bugger is everything we hate about the Indian state,” Varma said. {079-C03}
On the bridge, Bota Singh and Garja Singh charged one paisa for a donkey and six for a cart. {#paisa} Every traveller paid.

Garja was happy with the money. Bota said they had come to be warriors, not traders, and since nobody paid them voluntarily, they were “like crooks or government”, which to him were synonyms. {#crooks}
Rent-seeking usually needs the state’s connivance, Varma said. Here apathy was enough: nobody asked who the two were, and the toll became normal.
## The losers’ version
History is normally told from the winner’s side, Varma said. The only accounts of the bridge come from the loser’s side, in Sikh books that treat the two men’s deaths as martyrdom. {079-C04}
~ That is why the fight reads, in his words, “like a Rajinikanth film”. Narrative battles are old too: after an earlier clash, the Mughals and the Sikhs each claimed to have won.

quote.text: What is curious is that history is normally told from the winner’s side.

sections.label: Third reel
sections.head: The engine and the eye
sections.caption: calculation and pattern recognition
body: Amit Varma’s chess film joins a novella to a life. In Stefan Zweig’s *The Royal Game*, Mr B is held by the Nazis in solitary confinement with nothing but a chess book, and plays against an alter ego until he is incredibly good.

Sultan Khan, the real-life Indian player, never read chess books or even talked chess with other players. Varma likened him to Viswanathan Anand, who, he once wrote, was taking a Maruti 800 into a Formula One race. {#maruti}
## Calculation and pattern

The two men stand for two routes to mastery. Varma cited Adriaan de Groot’s study: grandmasters and novices think the same number of moves ahead, but grandmasters are better at pattern recognition. {079-C05}

Mr B, after thousands of hours alone in a cell, calculates concrete lines almost like an engine. Khan has positional sense: he can look at a position on move eight and picture the pawn structure of the ending. {#move8}
In Varma’s ending, the two meet in Zweig’s match with the roles reversed, and Khan lets Mr B win.
~ Ajay Shah recalled real matches with a psychological edge, Fischer–Spassky and Gukesh–Ding. “Some matches are more normal than others, but these matches stick out.” {079-J16}

quote.text: He decides that he doesn’t want to win. That he wants to let this guy take it

portraits.hint: chess player from British India, British champion in 1928

sections.label: Fourth reel
sections.head: In strangers we trust
sections.caption: the trust capital of a country
body: Ajay Shah pitches the other way round. He sets up the rules of a situation, he said, “and then we require a genius like you to animate it with people and desires.” {079-C08}

His situation came from 19th-century America, where the post office created a public good: delivery of a packet anywhere in the United States at modest prices. {#postoffice} People posted potatoes and sacks of wheat, and the postal system moved the packets around.
## No rule against it
Almost as a joke, someone asked to post a child, and the clerks played along. As Amit Varma put it, there would have been no rule saying a parcel is not allowed to be human. {#rule}
The child was routed from one clearing centre to the next and, Shah thought, delivered to the grandparents. Posting children became a normal thing. {#normal}
For Shah, this said something about the country: parents, postal workers and children were all comfortable trusting the good behaviour of strangers. {079-C07}
~ He found it “so beautiful and so mind blowing” that there was this level of trust capital and good humour, and that postal employees would feed the children along the way.

quote.text: It speaks very well for the trust capital of that country.

side.boxText: Amit Varma explained the principle of the Russian short-story writer Anton Chekhov: if you show a gun in the first act, it must go off by the third. In the bill collector’s story, the wires, the Maggi and her neatness each pay off. {079-C01}

contQuote.text: Are we standing on one leg against the power of the state, I ask you, against the power of bad ideas? We shall continue to stand, it is all we can do.

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s first pitch, from a cinematographer’s dream
stories.head: Love in the time of late fees
body: It began with a dream. The show’s cinematographer, Vaishnav Vyas, told Amit Varma he had dreamt that Ajay Shah lived in a building and stole everybody’s bills.

Varma kept the premise. His hero, a geeky bachelor in his early fifties who looks like Shah, climbs the stairs of an oldish building that could be in Bandra East, picking up the bills on every doorstep. {#bandra}

Some residents with no bill forget to pay, and his friend from the electricity department cuts them off. Then the helpful “Ajay Bhai” gets the power back, for the bill amount, a late fee and a bribe, and the two split the proceeds.

A woman in her forties moves in alone. Her power is cut too, but she never comes to him: she is too ill to get out of bed. Touched, he gets it back and offers to make her dal chawal. Then he remembers, Varma said, “that like all men he has overpromised”. {079-J04}
She cooks for him in return, everything chopped into perfect pieces. At his flat, she tries to shut a bathroom cupboard that keeps springing open, and finds his hoard of bills, her own among them.

She storms out threatening to call the police, but never reports him. In the end she sees he meant no real harm, and he apologises clumsily. The details of how it resolves, Varma kept back, “partly because I haven’t thought of them yet”. {079-J06}
~ The last scene: doorbells ring across the building, the screen splits into many doors opening, and every bill is there. {#lastscene} The residents dance over the closing credits.
stories.why: Varma makes a petty rent-seeker sympathetic without a line of explanation. Every prop, from the wires to the Maggi to her tidiness, is planted early so that it can pay off later, as Chekhov advised. {079-C01}
stories.postscript: Vyas, who will play the rude nephew, offered to play the hero. Varma said no: “you’re too young and handsome.” {079-J02}

stories.start: So my story stars two young Saddhars in the eighteenth century, right?
stories.end: We shall continue to stand, it is all we can do.
stories.caption: Bota Singh and Garja Singh
stories.kicker: From Sarbpreet Singh’s history, two Sikhs and a toll
stories.head: Two men, one leg, no retreat
body: Amit Varma’s second story turns on 27 July 1739. The Sikhs of Punjab were in hiding from its Mughal governor, Zakaria Khan. Two young Sikhs, Bota Singh and Garja Singh, heard a farmer sneer that they were not lions but jackals. {#jackals}

Stung, they took an empty wooden bridge on the road from Delhi to Lahore and levied a Khalsa regime tax. {#khalsatax} Everyone paid. Bota wanted a fight, so he sent the governor a taunting letter in verse.

Zakaria Khan, bored, rode out with a hundred horses. In the Sikh accounts, the two beat back wave after wave until the Mughals shot them in the legs. With one working leg between them, they locked arms and fought on until they died. {#onelegged}
~ Varma invented only their inner lives: Bota the black sheep, Garja the rejected suitor.
stories.why: A story of alienation in the vein of Beckett and Stoppard: two young men who don’t know what they want die trying to prove something, to others and to themselves. {079-R02}

stories.start: So what I want to do here is I want to combine two stories.
stories.end: I think there is something truly fascinating here.
stories.caption: Sultan Khan and Mr B
stories.kicker: Amit Varma joins a Zweig novella to Sultan Khan’s life
stories.head: The champion who chose to lose
body: In Stefan Zweig’s novella *The Royal Game*, Mr B survives Nazi solitary confinement with only a chess book, playing an alter ego again and again.

Sultan Khan was real. Born in 1903, he mastered Indian chess, then the European game, and won the British Chess Championship in 1928, three times in all. {#threetimes} Then he came home and never played again.

In Amit Varma’s fiction, Khan’s father is the family’s black sheep, and the boy’s wins restore his standing. Every game becomes a fight for respect. Khan becomes world champion, meets Mr B in Zweig’s match with the roles reversed, and lets him win. The game he has played all his life, Varma said, “is not the game on the board. It is another game”. {079-S03}
~ Varma suggested the novella may deserve an episode of its own. {079-R05}
stories.why: Chess here is a way of finding out who you are. The real contest is the one inside each player’s head, and seeing that clearly can mean letting go of the win.

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s true story, with Amit Varma’s improvised drama
stories.head: Handle with care: contains child
body: In 19th-century America, Ajay Shah said, the post office offered delivery anywhere in the country at modest prices. People would post ten kilograms of potatoes or thirty kilograms of wheat. {#kilos}
Then, almost as a joke, someone asked to post a child. The clerks played along: they weighed the child, worked out the charges and pasted the address on the child’s shirt. {079-S05}
The child was passed from one clearing centre to the next like any parcel and delivered, Shah thought, to the grandparents. Soon posting children was normal.

~ Amit Varma supplied the drama: a drunk father posting his surly son on a pub bet, a storm, and a lonely old man in a sorting office who bonds with the parcel. “There is no protocol of who feeds a parcel,” he said. {079-J18}

quote.text: So they weighed the child and worked out the correct charges for the packet, and they said done.

stories.postscript: Shah left one question for another day: why universal delivery was a public good, not something markets supplied.

quiz.q: Whose dream gave Amit Varma the premise of a man who steals his neighbours’ bills?
quiz.a: Vaishnav Vyas, the show’s cinematographer, dreamt Ajay Shah was stealing everyone’s paperwork.

quiz.q: What, according to Amit Varma, does the bill collector share with the Indian state?
quiz.a: Rent-seeking, or hafta: he creates a problem and then charges to solve it.

quiz.q: What principle says a gun shown in the first act must go off by the third?
quiz.a: Chekhov’s gun, from Anton Chekhov: nothing in a story should be there without reason.

quiz.q: Why is the story of the Khalsa Bridge unusual among historical accounts?
quiz.a: The only accounts come from the losing side, Sikh texts that treat it as martyrdom.

quiz.q: What did Adriaan de Groot find about how far grandmasters and novices look ahead?
quiz.a: The same number of moves; grandmasters are better at pattern recognition.

quiz.q: What did Ajay Shah say posting children revealed about nineteenth-century America?
quiz.a: Its trust capital: parents, postal workers and children trusted the good behaviour of strangers.
